newsitem.title: CHINA: Japan party members talk security with China.
newsitem.headline: Japan party members talk security with China.

text.p: Defence policymakers from Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) on Friday began talks with Chinese leaders on bilateral and regional security issues, Japanese diplomats said.
Tokyo has been keen to soothe Chinese concerns over its plans for military cooperation with the United States under a new security alliance.

The Japanese delegation, led by former Foreign Minister and current head of the LDP foreign affairs research committee Taro Nakayama, was scheduled to meet Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen on Friday, the diplomats said.

The visit was a rare chance for senior LDP members to focus on security issues in discussions with top leaders in China, which sees any change in Japan's officially passive defence policy as a possible revival of World War Two-style militarism.
"I suppose they are going to explain the meaning of the new arrangement between Japan and the U.S.," said one Japanese diplomat.

The United States and Japan are reviewing defence cooperation after President Bill Clinton and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto agreed last year to redefine their bilateral security relationship for the post-Cold War era.

China is likely to be highly sensitive to any expansion of cooperation beyond the current guidelines laid down in 1978, which only cover contingency measures to respond to an attack on Japan by the former Soviet Union.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang this week warned Tokyo not to enlarge the scope of its security alliance with the United States.
He also called for Sino-Japanese talks to ease a dispute over the sovereignty of an uninhabited but potentially resource-rich island group in the East China Sea that is controlled by Tokyo.

Tensions over the islands, known in Japan as the Senkakus and in China as the Diaoyus, have risen in recent months after Japanese legislators prompted outrage in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan by visiting them to bolster Tokyo's claim.
Japanese coastguards last month mobilised a fleet of some 60 vessels to prevent Hong Kong and Taiwanese nationalist activists from landing on the group, which are also claimed by Taipei.
